distillation_scope: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for Acute hepatitis B. Exposure route, vaccination status, pregnancy, HIV/immunosuppression, viral genotype, coinfection, fulminant course, and chronicity are represented as context, mechanisms, axes, risks, or treatment modifiers rather than disease-name qualifiers.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Acute acquisition or newly active replication of hepatitis B virus in hepatocytes with circulating HBsAg, HBeAg in many cases, HBV DNA, and infected-hepatocyte antigen display.
Interferon, innate immune, and cytokine activity producing fever, malaise, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, headache, myalgia, and early systemic symptoms before or during jaundice.
HBV-specific cytotoxic T-cell and inflammatory hepatocyte injury. This immune clearance process drives high ALT/AST and symptoms while also enabling viral clearance in most immunocompetent adults.

Hepatocellular inflammation and canalicular dysfunction impair bilirubin handling, producing dark urine, scleral icterus, jaundice, pruritus, high total/direct bilirubin, and mild-to-moderate cholestatic enzyme elevation.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Acute hepatic synthetic failure and coagulopathy
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Severe hepatocyte injury reduces clotting-factor synthesis and hepatic reserve, raising PT/INR and bleeding/procedure risk. It marks severe or fulminant acute hepatitis B when paired with encephalopathy or rapid deterioration.

Circulating HBV antigen-antibody immune complexes and complement activation producing serum-sickness-like rash, arthralgia, arthritis, low complement, and rarely vasculitic or renal manifestations around the preicteric or early icteric phase.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Fulminant necrosis and acute liver failure transition
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Massive/submassive hepatocyte necrosis and failing regeneration causing hepatic encephalopathy, hyperammonemia, cerebral edema, shock, AKI, bleeding risk, transplant need, and death hazard.
Coordinated immune control leading to falling HBV DNA, HBeAg loss, anti-HBe appearance, HBsAg clearance, anti-HBs development, and biochemical recovery.

Failure of durable immune clearance from infancy/childhood acquisition, HIV or immunosuppression, high inoculum, genotype or escape variants, coinfection, or impaired immune response, producing persistent HBsAg/HBV DNA beyond the acute episode.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Viral replication and antigenemia activate innate antiviral symptoms.
HBV antigen display recruits adaptive immune hepatocyte injury.
Hepatocellular inflammation and canalicular dysfunction produce jaundice and direct hyperbilirubinemia.
Severe hepatocyte injury reduces synthetic reserve.
HBsAg, HBcAg, anti-HBV antibodies, and viral DNA can form immune complexes.
Progressive coagulopathy is a key transition toward ALF when hepatic reserve collapses.
The same adaptive response that injures hepatocytes usually clears HBV in immunocompetent adults.
Seroconversion and immune control lower HBV DNA and HBsAg burden.
Immune impairment or early-life acquisition reduces durable clearance.
HBsAg marks circulating HBV antigenemia.
HBeAg is often present during high-replication acute HBV, though not universal.
HBV DNA quantifies circulating viral replication.
IgM anti-HBc is the key acute HBV serologic response.
Anti-HBs rises after HBsAg clearance in recovery.
Successful immune clearance lowers viral load.
Fever can occur during the acute viral prodrome.
Measured fever may accompany symptomatic acute HBV.
Fatigue and malaise are common acute HBV symptoms.
Anorexia is a common acute hepatitis symptom.
Nausea and vomiting are common in symptomatic acute HBV.
Epigastric or right upper quadrant pain can accompany acute hepatitis.
Conjugated bilirubinuria produces dark urine.
Visible jaundice follows rising bilirubin.
Total bilirubin rises in icteric acute HBV.
Direct bilirubin rises with hepatocellular cholestasis.
ALT is typically markedly elevated in acute HBV hepatitis.
AST rises with hepatocellular injury.
Reduced hepatic clotting-factor synthesis prolongs INR.
Immune-complex serum-sickness-like activity can produce rash.
Arthralgia or arthritis can accompany acute HBV immune-complex disease.
Complement consumption may lower C4 in serum-sickness-like presentations.
Massive hepatocyte necrosis can transition to ALF.
Fulminant HBV can cause hepatic encephalopathy.
Severe hepatic failure impairs ammonia detoxification.
ALF and shock can cause AKI.
Fulminant hepatitis B is the dominant acute mortality pathway.
Persistence pressure raises risk of HBsAg/HBV DNA persistence beyond six months.

axes.shape_free_text: Days from first systemic symptom, dark urine, rash/arthralgia, or jaundice to current observation.
Recent sexual exposure, needle sharing, blood exposure, occupational exposure, household contact, piercing/tattoo, or other plausible HBV acquisition context.
Context that vaccination did not generate durable protective anti-HBs or that immune escape/waning allowed infection despite prior vaccination.
HBsAg positivity during acute infection; may clear during recovery.
HBeAg positivity reflecting active replication in many acute HBV cases; absent in some precore/core-promoter variants.
Anti-HBe positivity during recovery or HBeAg-negative infection context.
IgM anti-HBc positivity supporting acute or recent HBV infection; low-level positivity can also appear in some reactivation contexts.
IgG/total anti-HBc positivity after HBV exposure; accompanies acute infection and remains after recovery.
Anti-HBs level; low or absent during acute infection, rising after recovery, or present before infection in vaccine breakthrough/escape contexts.
HBV DNA viral load. Values reported in IU/mL can be converted to copies/mL when needed for a common axis.
HIV with low CD4 count, transplant drugs, chemotherapy, biologics, high-dose steroids, or other cellular immune impairment altering acute HBV severity and clearance.
Subjective or documented fever during the acute viral prodrome or immune-complex phase.
Measured temperature; can be normal despite active hepatitis.
Heart rate; rises with fever, dehydration, pain, shock, or severe systemic illness.
Mean arterial pressure; usually preserved in uncomplicated acute HBV and falls with ALF shock, sepsis, bleeding, or dehydration.
Malaise, fatigue, asthenia, or reduced activity during acute HBV.
Reduced appetite or food aversion during acute hepatitis.
Nausea, vomiting, or poor oral intake.
Epigastric, right upper quadrant, or diffuse abdominal pain from acute hepatitis, capsule stretch, nausea, ascites, or overlap mimics.
RUQ pain or hepatic tenderness in acute hepatitis B.
Dark urine from bilirubinuria in icteric hepatocellular disease.
Visible jaundice or scleral icterus from acute HBV cholestatic dysfunction.
Itching during cholestatic/icteric acute hepatitis.
Rash during acute HBV, often serum-sickness-like, erythematous, macular, maculopapular, urticarial, petechial, or purpuric.
Painful/pruritic non-blanching macular, urticarial, or maculopapular rash consistent with HBV immune-complex serum-sickness-like reaction.
Joint pain, stiffness, or tenderness during acute HBV prodrome or immune-complex disease.
Objective polyarthritis, joint swelling, effusion, restricted motion, or symmetric small-joint involvement during HBV serum-sickness-like reaction.
AST rises with acute hepatocellular injury; may exceed 1000 U/L in severe or fulminant acute HBV.
ALT is often the dominant aminotransferase in acute HBV and can reach the thousands.
LDH can rise with severe hepatocellular necrosis, ischemic physiology, or hemolysis overlap.
Total bilirubin in icteric acute HBV, sometimes very high in severe cholestatic or ALF presentations.
Direct bilirubin fraction from hepatocellular cholestasis and impaired excretion.
ALP is usually normal to mildly elevated in hepatocellular acute HBV; high values should raise biliary/infiltrative mimic context.
GGT can rise with cholestasis, alcohol, medication, or biliary overlap.
INR rises with acute hepatic synthetic dysfunction; severe prolongation is a key ALF and transplant-context signal.
Measured PT in seconds when INR is unavailable.
Albumin usually remains near baseline in hyperacute illness but falls with inflammation, dilution, chronic liver disease, or prolonged severe hepatitis.
Ammonia rises when acute HBV progresses to ALF with detoxification failure.
WBC is nonspecific; may be normal, low with viral illness, or high with stress/coinfection.
Platelets are often normal but may fall with severe liver failure, DIC, hypersplenism, coinfection, or immune phenomena.
CRP is usually modest in uncomplicated viral hepatitis and higher with immune-complex inflammation or bacterial mimic.
ESR can rise in immune-complex or inflammatory presentations but is nonspecific.
C3 may be normal or low in HBV immune-complex serum-sickness-like disease.
C4 may be consumed in immune-complex serum-sickness-like disease.
Creatinine rises with ALF-associated AKI, hypovolemia, hepatorenal physiology, vasculitis/immune-complex renal disease, or drug toxicity.
BUN rises with dehydration, renal dysfunction, bleeding, catabolism, or AKI in severe acute hepatitis.
Hypoglycemia may occur in ALF; stress hyperglycemia or dextrose treatment can also alter values.
West Haven or equivalent hepatic encephalopathy grade in fulminant acute HBV.
Risk of transition to acute liver failure with coagulopathy plus encephalopathy, cerebral edema, or transplant-level deterioration.
Risk of encephalopathy emerging from ALF physiology.
Risk of cerebral edema or intracranial hypertension in severe ALF.
AKI hazard from ALF, shock, dehydration, renal immune-complex disease, or nephrotoxic context.
Major bleeding hazard from severe coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, DIC overlap, procedures, or liver failure.
Hazard that HBsAg/HBV DNA persists beyond six months after acute HBV presentation.
Lifespan-only mortality hazard emerging from fulminant hepatitis, cerebral edema, shock, bleeding, AKI, infection, transplant infeasibility, and host reserve.

Context for HBV-active nucleos(t)ide therapy: severe or fulminant hepatitis, rising INR/bilirubin, protracted severe course, very high viral load, immunosuppression, pregnancy, transplant consideration, or inability to tolerate deterioration.
Probability that current antiviral regimen has meaningful HBV activity, such as tenofovir, entecavir, or lamivudine.
Need to adjust nucleos(t)ide dosing or choose agent based on kidney function.
Need for urgent transplant-center discussion or listing when acute HBV becomes fulminant or high-risk severe hepatitis.
Feasibility of rescue liver transplant based on medical, psychosocial, center, donor, infection, malignancy, neurologic, or hemodynamic context.
Feasibility of therapeutic plasma exchange as bridge/support in fulminant liver failure context.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: ALT and AST rise together from hepatocellular injury, with ratio modulated by severity and comorbidity.
Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia produces bilirubinuria and dark urine.
Rising INR is a central severity signal for acute liver failure.
Severe synthetic failure increases bleeding and procedural risk.
High-grade encephalopathy signals cerebral edema risk in ALF.
Hyperammonemia contributes to encephalopathy, though exam is modulated by sedatives, fever, shock, and cerebral edema.
Fulminant acute hepatitis B drives short-term death risk.
Cerebral edema and herniation physiology are high-lethality ALF complications.
AKI worsens acid-base, volume, and toxin/ammonia control in ALF.
Major bleeding in ALF can be fatal or block procedures/transplant.
Rash and arthralgia often co-occur from immune-complex extrahepatic activity.
C4 consumption supports immune-complex serum-sickness-like activity.
Anti-HBs usually rises after HBsAg clears during recovery.
Persistent HBV DNA late after presentation increases chronicity risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Supportive outpatient-level care is insufficient when ALF physiology is active.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduces physiologic stress and preserves oral intake while immune clearance and monitoring define the course.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Replication suppression matters most when severe, fulminant, protracted, immunosuppressed, pregnant, or transplant-level context is active.
Kidney dysfunction affects tenofovir formulation and dosing safety.

side_effects.interpretation: Tenofovir toxicity or renal handling effects are context dependent and require monitoring.

treatments.context_specific_role: Suppresses HBV replication and can reduce progression pressure when severe acute HBV or high-risk host context is active.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Entecavir requires renal dose adjustment but can be chosen when tenofovir toxicity context is unfavorable.

treatments.context_specific_role: Potent HBV-active oral antiviral option when acute HBV severity or host context makes viral suppression outcome-relevant.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: High viral load provides room for observable suppression.

treatments.context_specific_role: HBV-active antiviral with historical acute severe HBV use; effect emerges through viral-load suppression rather than a semantic rank label.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: High-grade encephalopathy activates airway, cerebral edema, ammonia, glucose, sodium, and ICU monitoring interventions.

treatments.context_specific_role: Stabilizes ALF physiology while viral suppression, native recovery, transplant path, or bridge therapies are evaluated.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Transplant pathway changes outcome only when native recovery is unlikely or ALF is severe.
Medical, neurologic, infection, psychosocial, center, or donor constraints can prevent transplant delivery.

side_effects.interpretation: Perioperative bleeding risk depends on coagulopathy and operative context.
Post-transplant HBV prophylaxis/suppression context becomes mandatory.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue pathway for fulminant acute hepatitis B with poor native recovery signals.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: TPE requires access, blood-product availability, center capability, and hemodynamic tolerance.
Bridge/support becomes more relevant when transplant cannot be promptly delivered.

side_effects.interpretation: Central access, anticoagulation, and plasma exposure can add procedure-related risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Extracorporeal bridge/support in fulminant acute HBV physiology, selected by context axes rather than a fixed label.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises acute HBV prior when compatible prodrome, jaundice, transaminitis, or acute serology is present.
Increases susceptibility to acquisition despite exposure; breakthrough infection can still occur with documented prior vaccination.
Adults more often have symptomatic icteric hepatitis and usually clear infection.
Early-life acquisition is often less icteric but much more likely to persist chronically.
Impaired cellular immunity can alter serology, allow high viremia, reduce clearance, and increase fulminant or persistence risk depending on immune state and viral factors.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Immunosuppression makes viral suppression and durable HBV-active therapy more outcome-relevant.
HBV-active suppression is more important when immune clearance is impaired.

present.trajectory_modulation: Pregnancy changes safety thresholds, transmission prevention, and antiviral context; severe hepatitis or high viral load raises maternal-fetal risk.

treatment_effect_modulation.clinical_rationale: Tenofovir-based HBV suppression may be selected when maternal severity or transmission-risk context is active.

present.trajectory_modulation: EBV, HCV, HDV, HIV, alcohol-related liver disease, fatty liver, or other liver disease can increase severity, complicate serology, and alter chronicity or recovery.
Viral variants can produce HBeAg-negative acute hepatitis, vaccine breakthrough, severe immune escape, or fulminant patterns.
Delayed care with rising bilirubin/INR increases ALF and transplant-pathway context.

supportive_care: Track illness phase with serial symptoms, bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR/PT, mental status, glucose, creatinine/BUN, platelets, and HBV serology/DNA rather than a single snapshot.

Preserve HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, HBeAg/anti-HBe, anti-HBs, and HBV DNA as microbiology axes; final paper diagnosis and later seroconversion should stay confirmatory in case files when testing presentation-time ranking.
Evaluate for acute liver failure whenever INR rises, mental status changes, glucose falls, ammonia rises, creatinine worsens, or bilirubin/aminotransferases deteriorate.
Avoid alcohol, acetaminophen overdose, unnecessary hepatotoxic drugs, and NSAID-heavy self-treatment when coagulopathy or renal risk is present.
Use abdominal ultrasound or other imaging to evaluate biliary obstruction, vascular thrombosis, ascites, or mimics; do not turn imaging exclusion of obstruction into a separate disease label.
For serum-sickness-like presentations, structure rash, arthralgia/arthritis, complement, urinalysis/renal involvement, and vasculitis mimic tests without deleting later hepatitis evidence.

For severe acute HBV, fulminant course, immunosuppression, pregnancy, protracted coagulopathy, or transplant consideration, allow HBV-active antivirals and ALF support to compete through forward outcome simulation.
Contact testing, vaccination, HBIG when indicated, counseling about sexual/blood exposure, and public-health reporting are prevention/context actions, not semantic shortcuts for diagnosis ranking.
When prior chronic HBV or reactivation is plausible, retain that context explicitly; do not force the same fact to be both acute HBV acquisition and a separate chronic-HBV landscape on the same axes.
quality_notes: The only disease-specific medical input for this distillation is the disease name: Acute hepatitis B.
